meaningMnemonic: This is the barracks radical. Do you see that soldier doing push-ups in front of the barracks? That's gonna be you if sarge finds out you skipped review duty.
The meaning of this radical is the same as the kanji. It means front .
If you were to look at a giant from above, this is what you would see. Do you see the head and two arms? The giant is facing towards the right.
I don't know what this thing is, but it's lovely . It has two eyes, a funny mouth, and a scraggly beard. It's lovely, and nothing else, okay? So remember it that way.

Do you see the big guy standing on top of that giant lip ring ? A little odd . Wait, is he using it as a diving board? Very odd. Does he want to jump into that odd-looking mouth beneath him? How supremely odd!
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means specialty .

Construction in the winter leads to aggression . Just think about it. It's cold, it's unpleasant, and you don't want to be there. So, you start to develop an aggression towards other people working with you on this winter project. Hints Imagine yourself walking through the winter construction site, taking out your aggression on anyone you see. You hate this winter construction!
readingMnemonic: You're taking your aggression out on everyone. Then, the sexy construction worker from WaniKani Level 1, こう いち , walks by without a shirt on. You take out all your aggression on him. Hints "Aggression" is going to depend on you, so you should imagine a scene where you take your aggression out on こういち , whatever that entails. Hint: When you see the radical construction ( 工 ) in a kanji, it will often take the こう reading.

meaningMnemonic: If someone is coming toward you in a car , holding a weapon in their hand , they're going to attack you! Hints Picture the car, weapon out the window, preparing to attack you full force!
readingMnemonic: Right before the attack begins, you recognize the hand holding this weapon and driving this car. It's Gecki ( げき ), your long-lost gecko who you may or may not have let fly off into a really fierce tsunami. Oops. I think he may be here attacking you out of revenge. Hints Gecki is attacking you now. He's hitting you over and over with his tiny car. He's yelling and smacking your ankles with his weapon. And all you can do is wait and let the attack happen, because you know you deserve it.

meaningMnemonic: After a tsunami , you find an axe on the ground next to some fins on the beach . The tsunami was pretty violent, and it looks like this axe got blown into some fish and cut off their fins and now those things are just on the ground by the beach. Hints See these things on the beach. It makes sense to see fins, as fins are usually in the ocean, so seeing them on the beach is logical. Pick up the stuff you find as you feel the beach sand between your toes.
readingMnemonic: Walking down the beach a bit more, you also find a hammer ( はま ). Gosh, looks like the tsunami hit a workshop or a hardware store or something. First the axe, now a hammer. Hints Pick up the hammer in your hand. It’s pretty heavy. The tsunami must have been very strong to pick up such a heavy hammer.

meaningMnemonic: This thread is odd , but that's what makes it beautiful . It's a little frayed, it's a little miscolored, but that's what makes it appealing to you. Hints If something is a bit odd, it's usually beautiful in its own way, just like this beautiful thread.
readingMnemonic: You take this beautiful thread and lock it up with a key ( き ). You want to keep it all to yourself, you want its beauty to be for your eyes only! Hints To remember that there's a beautiful thread hidden away, you tie a not-as-beautiful thread to the end of the key.

meaningMnemonic: There are some horns on the ground next to fins on a plate that are meant to benefit everyone. If you're a member of this town, one of your benefits is this little set up. Hints You pick up the horns off the ground and put them on your head, then eat some fins off the plate. This is just one of many benefits to living here. You'll never go hungry!
readingMnemonic: Another benefit is free 駅 ( えき ) usage! Whenever you come back home from places on the train, this 駅 is completely free. Hints Okay, so using the 駅 is probably a better benefit than eating cold fins off a plate on the ground, but you take what you can get. They're all free!

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami can't resist the call of a bog . Whenever a tsunami is headed toward land, a bog will always call out to it, "Hey tsunami, don't you want to hit me with your water? Come this way~" Hints Close your eyes and hear the bog's tempting call.
readingMnemonic: As you listen to the bog 's call you realize it looks just like the Numa ( ぬま ) Numa guy in your mind. You open your eyes and it's just a bog. You close your eyes, and there he is. The Numa Numa guy. Hints So that's what happened to him! If you're a youngun, just do a little Google and you'll be pretty pleased, I'm sure.

meaningMnemonic: Pointing your magic solar powered wishing stick at the sun , you attain the legs of a child . You’re old and want young legs to carry you around, so you took your wishing stick that’s powered by the sun, and you wished for the legs of a child. Hints Imagine yourself getting new legs. Legs that belong to a child. They’re limber and young and full of energy! Feel your legs of a child underneath you!
readingMnemonic: As you delight in your new legs, Je sus ( じ ) descends from the sky. “My child ,” he says, “why have you pointed the stick at the sun and wished for the legs of a child? You were already perfect, just as all of God’s children are perfect.” Hints Say back to Jesus, “I’m not your child Jesus! And you’re just jealous of my new legs! You wish you had the legs of a child, Jesus! Your legs are like super old!” Actually say this out loud, and remember how Jesus wishes he could be a child again too.

meaningMnemonic: Hold your fingers in front of you — whoa, you've got a complete set! Hints Think about how lucky you are to have a complete set of fingers as you hold them in front of you and admire them. Life would be a lot harder without a complete set of fingers.
readingMnemonic: To show off your complete set of fingers, you decide to play a solo ( そろ ) on the piano. Nothing demonstrates the capabilities of a complete set of fingers like a dazzling, rapid-fire piano solo. Hints Once you're done with your piano solo, you switch over to your guitar and play a solo on that too. Your complete set of fingers flies nimbly across the fretboard, and everyone oohs and aahs in admiration.

meaningMnemonic: What acts like a roof , a rib cage , and a safety net for your heart all at once? It's your country's constitution . Hints A good constitution should ensure you have a roof over your head, be sturdy like a rib cage, and provide some kind of safety net for the people and things closest to your heart, don't you think?
readingMnemonic: These days, constitutions need protection too. Your country's constitution is being protected by none other than Ken ( けん ) the samurai, hero for hire. Hints Picture Ken standing in front of your constitution. He'd better keep a close watch, though, 'cause wily ol' Nic Cage is in the business of thievin' on constitutions.

meaningMnemonic: You got your ice orders . Of course, your ice orders are to make things cool and cold . Hints Making things cool and cold are pretty much the only orders you'll hear from ice. Ice is very simple in that regard.
readingMnemonic: How will you make things cool and cold ? You'll use a special ray ( れい ) gun that shoots a cold ray. Hints Imagine a cold ray coming out of your ray gun. Anything it touches becomes cold. "Stay cool, bird boy," you say. Hint: When you see the radical orders ( 令 ) in a kanji, it's fairly likely the reading will be れい .

meaningMnemonic: A winter table would be an odd thing to deal with . Winter can be hard to deal with on its own, but turn your table into winter? Just dealing with your food getting cold would be the worst! Hints Look at this winter table. How are you ever going to deal with it? Just think of your favorite warm food and then imagine it getting cold. Deal with it, dog.
readingMnemonic: This winter table is something you have to deal with , sure, but what if you just gave it to a circus show ( しょ )? They like weird stuff like this. Hints Feel the relief of getting rid of this table. No more having to deal with it anymore. The circus show can have it.

meaningMnemonic: You loiter on the mountain , reading off the digits of pi on this winter morning. The cold mountain air is so delicate , and changes only in very tiny ways — just like pi when you add another digit to it. Hints What other delicate things and tiny changes would you notice on the mountain? A little bird alighting in a tree, or the snowflakes it shakes loose from a branch? That's for you to decide, but imagine it vividly whatever it is.
readingMnemonic: Ah! Of course! The delicate bumble be e ( び ). Slightly out of place in winter, but this tiny creature is your idea of delicate. It lands on your finger, and you look at every tiny fiber of its being. Hints Picture yourself looking at the bee, thinking how each hair on its body is so delicate and tiny. Maybe it has a delicate aroma to go with it. A slight smell of honey?

meaningMnemonic: You wear a great big cross with a drop on it, and head to a specialty exhibition for gambling . The big cross and drop on your chest is your badge for being admitted into the exhibition. Everyone at the specialty exhibition has a cross and drop, and everyone is gambling. Hints Picture yourself at this specialty exhibition. Feel the weight of the cross shaped badge on your chest as you continue gambling at the exhibition.
readingMnemonic: You’re not very good at gambling , but you are pretty good at cheating. You hack ( はく ) the specialty exhibition gambling machines to pay out lots of cash just for you. You hack quickly and quietly, so luckily no one notices that you’ve hacked the system. Hints Hack the gambling machines. Imagine the sounds of the exhibition around you as you work to hack the machines. Look at the computer parts and cables as you work.

meaningMnemonic: The Grain Mouth King pours grain from his mouth for you and his other subjects. You go to him and pull his finger. When you do this, grain pours from his mouth. But we were greedy. We didn't understand the extent to which we were harvesting his mouth wheat. Hints Of course, you need to imagine pulling the Grain Mouth King's finger, to some extent. You can't just read what we write for you, without going to the imagination zone. Pull that finger real hard a couple times, and watch an extra large purge of grain pour forth.
readingMnemonic: The extent to which we were harvesting grain from his mouth was too great. The Grain Mouth King has run out of grain. He worries he will lose power if he has no grain to offer, so he switches to barfing out ta ter ( てい ) tots instead. Hints Imagine hearing the rumors that the Grain Mouth King ran out of grain, so you go check the extent of his failure yourself. But tater tots taste pretty good too. Imagine eating one of his mouth tater tots and go ahead and comment about it to him.

meaningMnemonic: Ice from the east is frozen . Well, of course, all ice is frozen, but ice from the east is like, really super frozen. Hints Imagine this super frozen ice from the east. You’ve never seen anything quite like it before. It’s so frozen, it’s like it was frozen once and then frozen again. Twice frozen. Feel the ice and how freezing cold it is. It’s super cold, guys.
readingMnemonic: Japan is a country in the east, and this ice was frozen in とう きょう . とうきょう is really good at freezing frozen things, so it makes sense that this frozen ice came from there. Hints Imagine being in とうきょう and seeing all this frozen ice. Hear people speaking Japanese all around you as you touch and feel the freezing twice-frozen ice.

meaningMnemonic: The giant radical and the giant kanji are exactly the same! Massive!
readingMnemonic: Just recently, a giant rampaged through Little Kyo to ( きょ ), so now it's even smaller than before. Poor Little Kyoto. Hints See Little Kyoto after the giant rampaged through it. It looks even smaller and more pathetic than ever. Look at all the smoldering rubble and smell the smoke with your nose.

meaningMnemonic: Only give grain s to a turkey if it's immature . Adult turkeys should be eating healthier things, like insects and grass. But immature turkeys don't care if they get fat, so they whine and whine and whine until you give them grains. Hints Imagine an immature turkey complaining at you until you give it grains. Now it's taking selfies with the grains and posting pics to Instagram and hashtagging them #GRAINLIFE.
readingMnemonic: Another thing immature turkeys (and people) love is chee se ( ち ). Most of us non-immature people and birds still like cheese, but if you didn't have an immature cheese phase as a kid or teen, you won't be able to like cheese as a mature old person. Hints Imagine a bunch of immature kids and turkeys eating cheese together.

meaningMnemonic: Super poop is a super power you have in infancy . Those in infancy have the power to poop at will, whenever and wherever they please. Infancy poop power! Hints Infants poop a lot. There's poop everywhere. The powerful aroma overwhelms you. Eww. Also refers to childhood, when you still have some of your poop powers, but they're already starting to go away.
readingMnemonic: In infancy , one eats a lot of soft foods, such as yo gurt ( よう ). Yogurt is the food item above all others that grants superior pooping power. Hints See this infant gobbling up all the yogurt he can get his grubby little hands on. Soon, he begins to poop all over the place. Hear the infant screaming, "Goo-goo! Yogurt poop power! I'm a baby! Wahhhh!!"

meaningMnemonic: See that woman with the broom ? That's the lady of the house. She's getting ready to hand that broom to you — her butler — because you missed a spot over there. Hints The lady of the house will tolerate nothing less than excellence, so get ready to sweep and re-sweep this floor till you meet your lady's expectations.
readingMnemonic: Instead of your name, the lady of the house just calls you " foo l" ( ふ ). You rarely meet her ladyship's lofty standards, so from her perspective you're just a silly nincompoop fool who can't get anything right. Hints "You there — fool. Come sweep this floor again." "Yes, m'lady — your humble fool lives to serve, m'lady."

meaningMnemonic: You stick horns in the ground using them as spikes and you line up the horns in a straight line. Horns are pretty much the same thing as spikes once you stick them in the ground, and you line these ones up precisely for optimal protection. Hints Imagine yourself lining up these horns in the ground. The spikes are sharp and you poke yourself with one. Ouch. Need to be more careful as you line these up.
readingMnemonic: As you line up these horns and stick them into the ground, you notice a bull munching on hay ( へい ) nearby. It's staring at the horns you're lining up. Somehow it feels like it's munching that hay angrily. You gulp, looking at its horn as it grabs another mouthful of hay, and you feel pretty guilty. Hints Imagine the hay in that bull's mouth as it chomps angrily, watching you line up horns in the ground. It probably wishes you were the hay.

meaningMnemonic: If you know the radical meaning lovely , you know the kanji meaning lovely as well! Hints You know what would make learning this kanji lovely? Studying your radicals.
readingMnemonic: " Lovely " is the name of my ray ( れい ) gun. It's more lovely than any other thing. Hints Try to imagine feeling this way about your ray gun. It's so lovely.

meaningMnemonic: Your leader is using a stick in the winter made of hair . This is the stick of mastering and repair . Hints Imagine your leader holding this stick of hair in the winter, going around mastering all kinds of skills and repairing everything in sight. What a strange stick, giving even stranger abilities to its wielder.
readingMnemonic: What's the key to mastering any skill? A stick and a shoe ( しゅう )! Hints Picture your leader again; stick in one hand, shoe in the other. He looks kind of threatening, like he's about to slap you with the stick and then throw the shoe at you. But that's what it takes for mastering certain skills. This is all for discipline’s sake.

meaningMnemonic: The odd radical and the odd kanji are the same. They're both... really strange . Hints Remember how odd this one is?
readingMnemonic: You're odd too, just like this kanji. But you don't want anyone to know, so you lock away your strange habits with a key ( き ). Hints You only give this odd key to people you trust, so they can unlock your odd secrets and see how odd you are deep down.

meaningMnemonic: A woman is one of the few peculiar things in the world. Everything but a woman can be explained and made sense of. There are only a few truly peculiar things in this world, with woman being one of them. Hints Imagine saying this to a woman. Try and imagine her face as you tell her how peculiar she is.
readingMnemonic: But when you think about it, we're all a little peculiar. Me, you, myou ( みょう ) everybody! Hints Who's peculiar? Me and you. Me, you — we are peculiar! Peculiar, peculiar, peculiar!

meaningMnemonic: Blood and hair and tofu make up the populace . Those are the three categories the entire populace fits into, anyway. Hints Blood shows that all the people are related. Hair shows that we're all humans. Tofu is food to all. So, as you can see, those three words describe the entire populace.
readingMnemonic: The entire populace deserves shoe s ( しゅう ). It's a basic thing all humans should have like flowing blood, hair (somewhere), and tofu to eat. Hints If you see people in your populace without shoes, it's your job as a fellow member of society to help them get some!

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami that's blue is pure . Some tsunami are other colors, like brown or red because they aren't pure, they'll full of trash and poop and other horrible things. But a blue tsunami is completely pure! Hints Picture this pure blue tsunami. You can see every crystal clear drop of water in it.
readingMnemonic: Seeing this pure blue tsunami inspires you to pull out your glowing blue sa ber ( せい )! As the pure water comes toward you, you take one, long slash! Hints SPLAASHH! The tsunami's pure water splits and it absorbed into your saber. Now it's pure too. And transparent!

meaningMnemonic: When a tsunami cuts through your rib cage like a sword through thread , it leaves you feeling pure and clean . Hints Imagine a tsunami-level rib cage rinse — the water rushing between your rib bones and washing out all the crevices. You'd feel pretty pure and clean after that, right?
readingMnemonic: After the tsunami pulls away, your insides are left so pure and clean that they're totally devoid of color. To fix this, you squirt ketsu p ( けつ ) all over them. That should turn them back to a healthy shade of red. Hints Before squirting the ketsup on your insides, you need to make sure it's clean and pure too. Only the cleanest, purest Heinz ketsup is sterile enough to squirt on your internal organs.

meaningMnemonic: A gold Wolverine swam in the water while his father made a record of it. Wolverine is gold in color because he just won the gold medal in swimming, so now he is gold. Way to go, Wolverine. Hints See this gold Wolverine holding his gold medal after getting out of the water. His dad doesn’t want to forget anything about this precious moment so he makes a record of it. Imagine him scribbling furiously in his notebook.
readingMnemonic: Since Wolverine is actually a mutant, he is soon disqualified from his gold medal. His father makes a record of this also. One angry fan threw a rock ( ろく ) at Wolverine afterwards. Then another threw a rock. And another rock. Before you knew it, everyone was throwing rocks at Wolverine. Wolverine’s dad didn’t step in to help though, he just kept keeping records. Hints Imagine a pitiful Wolverine crying on the ground as each rock hits him. All he wanted was some recognition from his father. Poor guy. Imagine poor Wolverine like this as his dad just looks on and writes in his notebook.

meaningMnemonic: If you ride your scooter while wearing horns in a barracks , you're going to get stuck and have to reverse out of there in the opposite direction. Hints Imagine riding your scooter to the barracks. It literally drops you on the ground when you get there, and then drives in reverse back the opposite way you came.
readingMnemonic: After you reverse in the opposite direction, you find a bunch of Gak ( ぎゃく ) covering your scooter wheels. The soldiers must have booby-trapped their barracks with Gak. You're able to reverse out of the barracks, but the Gak has gunked up your wheels so bad that they only go in reverse now. Weird… Guess you'll be going in reverse forever. Hints If you don’t know what Gak is, check out this Gak commercial . The 90s were basically the heyday of non-Newtonian fluids masquerading as toys. Don't you wish you could reverse time and play with Gak again?

meaningMnemonic: A grain , from one evening to the next evening , experiences a shift . After two evenings, the grain has shifted from one location to another. Hints Picture the grain in your head with a time-lapse of one evening after another happening in the background. Slowly, the grain shifts.
readingMnemonic: This shift is caused by the ea gle ( い ) that wants to eat the grains. Every other evening, the eagle swoops down, shifts the grains (eating a few) and then flies off. Hints Picture the eagle flying down on the second evening, scattering the grains it doesn't eat, shifting their location.

meaningMnemonic: Rice that is blue has a strong spirit . Our spirits are blue, so if you ever see rice (or other food, or even people) that's blue, you know that's their spirit radiating out! Hints Picture this rice, the pulsing blue spirit of each grain is glowing so bright!
readingMnemonic: You want to see the spirit up close, so you take your sa ber ( せい ), throw the blue rice in the air, and slice it in half! The rice explodes and blue light fills everything! Then it's gone. Hints As you release the spirits in the rice, your saber begins to glow blue too. Their spirits are going inside your saber, making it stronger!

meaningMnemonic: This building features horns on a pig to represent our squad . Hints Our squad's symbol is horns on a pig, and we put it on everything to show the whole world our squad owns this turf.
readingMnemonic: Our squad also wears special tie s ( たい ) with our horned pig on it. And we don't care if you think that's lame, because we're A SQUAD. Hints Picture our squad. It's Koichi, Viet, the Crabigator and Tofugu. We're all wearing matching horned pig ties and walking toward you in slow motion, our squad building towering behind us with the pig smirking down at you.

meaningMnemonic: A canopy is over your car because your car is in storage in a large storehouse . Hints The canopy just protects your car from the elements as it sits in storage for long periods of time.
readingMnemonic: Your car is in this storage warehouse , just sitting there. A 子 ( こ ) notices this, and decides to take your car on a joyride. You won't notice, right? You never drive it. Hints Imagine a kid sneaking into your canopy to steal your car that's in storage. Maybe it's two 子 s, one stacked on the other with a trench coat. One 子 works the pedals while the other 子 works the steering.

meaningMnemonic: The gladiator in front of you draws his sword . He points the sword at your chest and right when you think everything is about to end, you realize he's pointing the sword at the ticket in your hand. Hints Right! You needed to buy a ticket to see the gladiator! He doesn't want to kill you, he wants to check to make sure you bought a ticket.
readingMnemonic: The gladiator happily marks your ticket with his blade, when Ken ( けん ) the samurai pushes past you. He holds up his own sword, challenging the gladiator, who just shakes his head and points at your ticket again. Hints Ken takes a long time to examine your ticket. I don't think he understands that he needs a ticket to fight the gladiator. Maybe you should give him yours.

meaningMnemonic: Using a hat , four person s with a cross make an umbrella . The hat is big enough to be an umbrella for all four people, so it makes sense. All four of them are religious missionaries, so that's why they're holding the cross under the "umbrella." Hints See these four people all under one makeshift umbrella. The giant hat is set atop the cross, which is what makes it kinda like an umbrella, and the four pairs of hands are all holding it upright.
readingMnemonic: You know the Spanish phrase "Mi casa ( かさ ) es su casa"? Well, this is kind of like that, but only with a hat. And that hat is also an umbrella . Mi casa es yours too, because it's an umbrella and also a hat. This makes sense, trust me. Hints Imagine the four people in the umbrella hat again, only this time imagine them skipping along singing "Mi casa es su casa." It'll help you remember.

meaningMnemonic: You advance and attack ! This is a charge on someone or something, though it can also be an advance on them. Yep, this is the 進撃 from 進撃の巨人 , the popular anime and manga. Don't say you never learned anything useful here.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the ones you learned with the kanji. Advance! Charge! Move on to the next item!

sentences.japanese: どうにかして敵の進撃をはばんでくれ！
sentences.english: Do something to halt the enemy's advance!

sentences.japanese: ビエトは敵に進撃した。
sentences.english: Viet advanced on the enemy.

sentences.japanese: 進撃の巨人にはまっています。
sentences.english: I’m hooked on Attack on Titan.

sentences.japanese: いやー、すごいですね！阪神タイガースの快進撃！この進撃、続いてほしいですね。
sentences.english: Wow, isn't that amazing? That Hanshin Tigers' incredible winning streak! I really hope this momentum continues.

meaningMnemonic: What's a before sell ticket ? It's a ticket you sell before an event. In other words, an advance ticket or a ticket sold in advance ! 前売り券 are often tickets with reduced prices and certain benefits or perks. Note that you'll also see this written as 前売券 , without the okurigana, but the reading will stay the same.
readingMnemonic: The readings are 前 , 売る and 券 combined into one awkward word.

sentences.japanese: 前売り券はどこで買えるんですか？
sentences.english: Where can I buy advance tickets?

sentences.japanese: 映画の前売り券を二枚もらったんだけど、よかったらいっしょに行かない？
sentences.english: I got two advance tickets for a movie. Would you like to come with me?

sentences.japanese: ディスカウントも特典もないんなら、前売り券を買う意味なくない？
sentences.english: If there are no discounts or special offers, what's the point of buying advance tickets?

sentences.japanese: 前売り券は他の割引とは併用できませんって書いてあるよ。
sentences.english: It says that tickets sold in advance can't be used with other discounts.

meaningMnemonic: This is the adverb version of 再 , so it shares the meaning again and also has the meaning once again . Note that this word is somewhat formal and literary.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Once again , you have to say " Who ? Ta - ta !" ( ふたた ). That's because people you don't know keep trying to talk to you, again and again. Whenever this happens you say "Who? Ta-ta!" again and run away.

sentences.japanese: 男はよろめきながらも、再びゆっくりと歩き始めた。
sentences.english: The man, though staggering, began to slowly walk once again.

sentences.japanese: この地を再び訪れることになるとは思ってもいなかったよ。
sentences.english: I didn't think I would end up visiting this place again.

sentences.japanese: 次の朝、怪物は再び現れた。
sentences.english: The next morning, the monster appeared again.

meaningMnemonic: A giant person is a giant .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 虫にとっては、人間も巨人でしょ。
sentences.english: To insects, humans are giants, right?

sentences.japanese: えっ、巨人ファンなんですか？
sentences.english: What, are you a Giants fan?

sentences.japanese: あのバスケットボール選手は巨人症です。
sentences.english: That basketball player has gigantism.

meaningMnemonic: The army squad is an army . It's also just the army . It refers more to "an" army rather than "the" army. Just a group of people who do army things.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 軍隊ごっこをしているの？面白そう。私も入れてよ。
sentences.english: Are you playing army? That looks fun. Let me in too.

sentences.japanese: 私は、軍隊を持つ必要の無い国は存在しないと思っています。
sentences.english: I do not believe that there is any country that does not need to have an army.

sentences.japanese: この世代の男性は軍隊経験がある人が多いんです。
sentences.english: Many men of this generation have military experience.

meaningMnemonic: 矢印 combines the kanji arrow and the vocab word 印 (mark), giving us the type of arrow you use for pointing at things, like these: →↑↓←. It could be an arrow on a sign, or on a piece of paper, or a document. We can just call it an arrow , or an arrow symbol .
readingMnemonic: The reading is 矢 and 印 put together into one. The 印 is like the actual vocab word 印 , but watch out for rendaku changing it from しるし to じるし .

sentences.japanese: 矢印にそって進んでください。
sentences.english: Please follow the arrows.

sentences.japanese: あの矢印の道路標識は何という意味ですか。
sentences.english: What does the arrow road sign mean?

sentences.japanese: 矢印ってどうやって出すの？
sentences.english: How do you make the arrow symbols appear?

sentences.english: The blue arrow road sign means "left turn allowed," and the sign with a white arrow on a blue background means "one-way"!

meaningMnemonic: Gold storage is where you put your gold. You want it to be safe, so you put it in a safe or a vault . 金庫 can refer to various types of secure storage. Depending on the context, it can mean a personal safe, a bank vault, or a safety deposit box.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 家に金庫はありますか？
sentences.english: Do you have a safe in your home?

sentences.japanese: マミは貸金庫にベーコンをあずけているらしいよ。
sentences.english: Apparently Mami keeps her bacon in a safe-deposit box.

sentences.japanese: あの銀行の金庫はとても頑丈です。
sentences.english: That bank vault is very sturdy.

meaningMnemonic: 占い is "fortune telling." Star fortune telling is when you use the stars for fortune telling. That's known as astrology or horoscope .
readingMnemonic: The reading is the words 星 and 占い put together into one. Did you foresee that one coming?

sentences.japanese: 毎日朝の番組で今日の星占いを見てから学校に行きます。
sentences.english: Every day, I watch the day’s horoscope on the morning TV show and then head to school.

sentences.japanese: 「星占いを信じるとか、バカみたい」ってむすめには冷たく言われるんだけど、ついつい見ちゃうんだよね。
sentences.english: My daughter coldly says that it's stupid to believe in horoscopes, but I can't help looking at them.

sentences.japanese: 今日の星占いで、頭にたんこぶができないように気をつけた方がいいと出ていたの。
sentences.english: Today's horoscope said I should be careful not to get a bump on my head.

meaningMnemonic: With aggression you attack the enemy. This is an attack . 攻撃 usually refers to attacking someone or something with the intent of causing direct harm or damage, either physically or verbally. You'll hear it used in the context of war, games, arguments, or even things like media criticism or cyberattacks.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: サーバーがサイバー攻撃を受けている。
sentences.english: The server is under cyber attack.

sentences.english: The enemy will probably attack the megacities first.

sentences.japanese: 後ろから攻撃を仕掛けてくるなんて、ひきょうだぞ！
sentences.english: You are such a coward to make a surprise attack from the back.

sentences.english: It was the sexiest missile attack I've ever seen.

sentences.japanese: 昨日、武力攻撃が開始された。
sentences.english: Yesterday, an armed attack was launched.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. It's worth mentioning that a more common way to say beach is ビーチ , and many people actually say 海 even though this literally means "sea."
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

sentences.japanese: さっき、浜でモクズガニを見ました！

sentences.japanese: え、浜さんもこの日、浜にいたんですか？
sentences.english: What, were you also on the beach that day, Hama-san?

sentences.english: I heard that when a baby dolphin washed up on the beach, the local people returned it to the sea.

meaningMnemonic: This is like saying "when it comes to the 何故 ," which means you're giving a reason, making this because or the reason is , followed by… whatever you wanna say! Note that this is a quite formal way to say "because," so you'll mostly encounter this in writing or formal speech, and almost always at the beginning of a sentence in Japanese.
readingMnemonic: This reading is an exception but you learned them already because they're the same as the word 何故 , which you learned a few levels ago. It just has some kana attached to it!

sentences.english: It's because you should use your waiting time more productively.

sentences.japanese: 何故なら、彼は魔法使いだったのです。
sentences.english: Because, he was a wizard!

meaningMnemonic: To have benefit is to be beneficial . 有益 is a more formal word than 役に立つ (useful). It's often used for things like 有益なアドバイス (beneficial advice) or 有益な情報 (useful information).
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 有益なアドバイス、有難うございます。
sentences.english: Thank you for your beneficial advice.

sentences.japanese: ビジネスをするなら、社会にとって有益なサービスでないと、意味がないと思うんです。
sentences.english: I think that if you are going to do business, it must be a beneficial service to society, otherwise it is meaningless.

sentences.japanese: 非常に有益な情報を提供していただき、有り難うございます。
sentences.english: Thank you very much for your very useful information.

meaningMnemonic: A 間違い is a mistake. A big mistake is a big mistake . 大間違い is less about factual errors and more about someone being way off in their assumptions or expectations. It suggests things didn't go according to plan — like you assumed a smile would fix everything or expected a date to go well, only for things to turn out completely wrong.
readingMnemonic: The reading is 大 and 間違い put together into one not so mistaken word.

sentences.japanese: ニコニコ笑っておけば何とかなるでしょって思ってる人は大間違いですよ。
sentences.english: Those who think they can get by if they just smile and laugh are very mistaken.

sentences.japanese: そもそも、野外で録音しようとしたのが大間違いだった。
sentences.english: The original big mistake was that we tried to record outdoors.

sentences.japanese: これで夏が終わったと思ったら大間違いだよ！本当の夏は、まだまだこれからなんだから。
sentences.english: If you think this is the end of summer, you are mistaken! The real summer is yet to come.

sentences.japanese: 彼女をデートに誘ったが、それは大間違いだった。
sentences.english: I asked her to go out with me, but it was a big mistake.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how the vocab 身 means "body" and 振る means "to shake something"? Well, the way you "shake" your body is your body language , or how you gesture . 身振り generally refers to body movements and gestures that make communication more expressive or help bridge language barriers. You'll often encounter this together with 手振り (hand gestures) in the phrase 身振り手振り .
readingMnemonic: The reading for this is the kun'yomis for 身 and 振る put together, where the 振り gets rendaku'd to ぶり .

sentences.japanese: 日本人の人たちと、身振り手振りで何とかコミュニケーションをとることができた。
sentences.english: I managed to communicate to Japanese people with gestures.

sentences.japanese: あの子って、いつも身振り手振りが大げさなんですよね。
sentences.english: That girl is always exaggerating her gestures and body language.

sentences.japanese: ビエトは部下に、どこかに隠れるよう身振りで合図した。
sentences.english: Viet motioned to his men to hide somewhere.

sentences.japanese: 男は肩をすくめて「それで？オレは知らねーよ？」という意味の身振りをした。
sentences.english: The man shrugged his shoulders, making a gesture that meant, "So what? I don't know anything about it, okay?"

meaningMnemonic: Many times is how many times you can use this number of ticket s. That means there are many tickets, making this a book of tickets . 回数券 refers to a book or set of prepaid tickets that are often sold at a discount and can either be physical or digital. They are commonly used for public transportation, like buses or trains, and can also be issued by other businesses that people frequent, such as hot springs and public baths.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 回数券だと、どれくらい安くなりますか？

sentences.japanese: 電車の回数券は金券ショップでも買えますよ。
sentences.english: You can also buy a book of train tickets from a ticket outlet.

meaningMnemonic: お菓子 is "candy," right? Add store onto that and you have a candy store .
readingMnemonic: This word uses the readings you learned with the kanji. It will help to know the word お菓子 as well.

sentences.english: I bought this canelé from my favorite local pastry shop.

sentences.english: Among the candy shops, there are several types, such as Japanese sweet stores and Western sweet stores.

meaningMnemonic: You have 時代 as a "period" of time you're talking about. What period? The infancy year s. Those years are not just when you're a baby, but when you were growing up too. That was your childhood . 幼年時代 specifically means your early childhood years. It's a formal, slightly stiff word you mostly see in writing, often appearing in literature, autobiographies, or memoirs looking back on someone's younger years.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 『幼年時代』って、トルストイの幼年時代の思い出について書かれた本じゃないんですか？
sentences.english: Isn't "Childhood" a book about Tolstoy's childhood memories?

sentences.japanese: その時私は、あの幸せな幼年時代は、もう二度と帰ってはこないんだと実感しました。
sentences.english: At that moment I realized that those happy childhood days would never come back.

sentences.japanese: 幼年時代の夏は、いつも九州の従兄弟のところで過ごしたから、ヒラタクワガタは思い出の虫なのだ。
sentences.english: I always spent my childhood summers at my cousin's place in Kyushu, so the flat stag beetle is a memorable bug for me.

meaningMnemonic: He who is both in his infancy and immature is probably childish and immature . When used as an adjective, 幼稚 describes negative immaturity in someone's behavior, remarks, or ideas. However, in compounds like 幼稚園 (kindergarten), it simply refers to the early childhood stage without any negative tone.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: うちの夫、本当に幼稚なんだよね。
sentences.english: My husband is really immature.

sentences.japanese: うちの子は今、土曜日の朝にある日本語学校の幼稚部に通っています。
sentences.english: My child is now attending the kindergarten section of a Japanese language school on Saturday mornings.

sentences.japanese: どうして幼稚な喋り方をする日本人女性が多いのですか？
sentences.english: Why do so many Japanese girls speak like children?

meaningMnemonic: The child who is a juvenile is just a child . A group of them is children . 児童 refers specifically to children who are of elementary school age, typically from around 6 to 12 years old. It's often used in formal contexts, like in legal documents or when referring to school children in educational settings.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: Ninety percent of the children were absent.

meaningMnemonic: Something so pure it's pure twice. It must be really clean ! Cleanliness is next to pure...liness, after all. I'm sure that's how the saying goes. 清潔 is a relatively formal word that refers to sanitary conditions in personal hygiene, public health, or medical settings. It can refer to both physically clean places and hygienic practices. In literature, 清潔 can also describe a person as morally pure.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: My type is a guy who is actually clean but looks dirty and sketchy.

meaningMnemonic: 比較 is a comparison. Add 的 to it and you have comparatively .

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 独り means "alone"? meaningMnemonic: You learned that 故 means reason. Basically, whatever comes before 故に in a statement is going to be the reason for something that comes after. So 故に works like therefore or consequently . It can also be translated as "because" or other similar conjunctions depending on the context. Also keep in mind that 故に is mainly used in formal contexts, like in academic writing or politicians' speeches — just like "therefore" in English.
readingMnemonic: By knowing the word 故 you'll know the reading for this word too! Here's a mnemonic in case you need a reminder, though: You're using WaniKani, therefore you're studying kanji and vocab. Whose fault is it? It's WaniKani's fault! But, your brain has been beaten to a mush from all the studying, so when you say "it's your fault" it comes out as "it's yue fault!" Go ahead and say it out loud that way.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 痛い is "painful"? It's a little more descriptive than 痛い , so you might see it used in writing or to describe a more persistent or recurring condition. It's also often used figuratively, especially in expressions like 心が痛む (my heart aches).

meaningMnemonic: You don't say "to aggression." When you do aggression on someone, you're probably doing something to hurt them in some way. It can also be used to describe taking bold actions, like moving ahead with a risky plan.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. So you can use 垂れる to describe your dog's floppy ears hanging down or your ice cream’s melty goodness dripping away. 垂れる is generally intransitive, but it can also take a direct object in specific expressions, like 説教を垂れる (to give a preachy lecture), こうべを垂れる (to bow one's head in humility), or the crude slang クソを垂れる (to drop a load).

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Your horse happened to twist his ankle, and he neigh ed ( ひね ) in discomfort. If it were you who had twisted your ankle, you probably would have screamed or shouted an expletive or something, but it's your horse, so he neighed. Poor guy. Put some ice on that thing for him. Note that this can also be read as ねじる , though this reading is usually written in kana. While ひねる refers to general twisting — like turning or bending to the side — ねじる tends to have a nuance of twisting something multiple times, like a string or wire, often from both ends.

meaningMnemonic: A peculiar drug that seems too good to be true? That's what we call a wonder drug or a miracle cure .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: ウナギは、昔から夏の暑さに負けないための妙薬として人気がありました。
sentences.english: Eels have long been popular as a wonder drug to beat the summer heat.

sentences.japanese: ホットワインは、ヨーロッパでは、風邪に効く妙薬としても知られています。
sentences.english: Hot wine is also known in Europe as a wonder drug for the common cold.

sentences.japanese: 古代中国では、水銀が不老長生の妙薬とされてきたって本当ですか？
sentences.english: Is it true that in ancient China, mercury was considered a wonder drug for longevity?

meaningMnemonic: If you long for something you'll get feelings of yearning and longing . Don't worry, some day you'll get whatever it is. 憧れ can also describe a strong feeling of admiration , particularly for people.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already so you should be able to read it!

sentences.japanese: 皆の憧れ
sentences.english: something or someone admired by all

sentences.japanese: 女性の憧れ
sentences.english: something or someone that women aspire to

sentences.english: to feel admiration for something or someone, to feel a longing for something or someone

sentences.english: to admire something or someone, to yearn for something or someone

sentences.english: to admire something or someone, to yearn for something or someone

meaningMnemonic: It's the side of the beach ! Well, wait, what is it? This will make better sense when you look at the reading for the word, since it's a place: Yokohama .
readingMnemonic: The reading is 横 and 浜 put together into one nice word, よこはま .

sentences.japanese: 横浜まで乗せてもらえませんか？
sentences.english: Could you give me a ride to Yokohama please?

sentences.japanese: 私は三ヶ月ほど横浜に住んでいたことがあります。
sentences.english: I once lived in Yokohama for about three months.

sentences.japanese: 横浜生まれ、横浜育ちの人のことを「浜っ子」って言うって本当ですか？
sentences.english: Is it true that people born and raised in Yokohama are called “Hamakko”?
